title: How the UK can revive tourism: cost, seasonality, places and people
label: 13 October 2026 · Tourism inquiry, oral evidence
summary: Witnesses described a tourism sector squeezed by rising costs, shorter and cheaper trips, and understaffing, while attractions and coastal towns need better marketing, joined-up public support, cleaner seas, improved transport and clearer rules on short-term lets; practical fixes proposed include extending seasons, better weather info, local control of levies, professionalising hospitality and resolving regulatory gaps for organisations like zoos.

speakers.label: Chris Haslam
speakers.name: Chris Haslam
speakers.role: Chief Travel Writer, The Sunday Times

chapters.title: How holiday habits and household finances have shifted
chapters.takeaway: People are taking shorter, cheaper trips, moving to self-catering and STRs, and this is squeezing hotels and attractions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To start: have tourists' expectations and priorities changed in recent years?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Yes. UK holidays are shorter — average now about 9.6 days overall and short breaks down from 3.3 to 2.9 days — and people are spending less since the 2021 post‑pandemic peak.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: There's a big shift toward short-term rentals (STRs), which now take around 20–25% of the market, with hotels down to about 40–45%.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Travellers want new experiences they can share on social media — not just lying on a beach. Families look for value and activities that keep kids entertained.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How are UK destinations responding to tighter household budgets?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Not well. Many places haven't adapted business models for shorter stays: spas, 24-hour dining or staff costs stay the same while spending per visitor falls.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Families increasingly choose self-catering to save money; online 'travel hacks' and budget tips are widespread to stretch holiday budgets.

chapters.title: Reviving coastal towns and managing seasonality
chapters.takeaway: Some towns succeed by attracting funding or engaging communities; extending the season is essential to sustainability.

turns.speaker: Mr Bayo Alaba
turns.text: What can seaside towns like Southend do to attract more overnight visitors?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Two models work: external funding and grants (Great Yarmouth) or community-led efforts (Bude). Both can revive a town if sustained and well managed.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: But the British seaside faces long-term decline: overnight stays down 18% in 10 years and many resorts are maintained for short summer seasons only.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Events help — music, food and local festivals bring day visitors who then return for longer stays; making places 'Instagrammable' also helps draw new crowds.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: Seasonality is the big issue. Extending shoulder months would help jobs and productivity — how do we do it with unpredictable UK weather?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Extend the season with new products — 'coolcations' for people escaping hotter summers abroad, wetsuits for kids, autumn festivals — and better marketing.

chapters.title: Experience, cleanliness and environmental confidence
chapters.takeaway: Visitors care about cleanliness, public facilities and safe bathing water — sewage discharges and closed toilets put people off.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: What practical things make a place stand out?

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Cleanliness, helpful staff, activities for children, clear information or an app — those add value beyond the headline price.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Simple basics matter: clean toilets, emptied bins, fair car parking and functioning services — failing these angers visitors more than fancy attractions.

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: A major barrier is bathing-water quality. Sewage discharges (CSOs) and reports of pollution put people off going to the sea.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: DEFRA posts seasonal testing results, but those are historic; CSO discharges happen unpredictably. Many rely on apps like Surfers Against Sewage to check real-time safety.

chapters.title: Digital discovery, influencers, AI and weather information
chapters.takeaway: Social media drives discovery more than official promotion, AI will change planning, and better weather icons could stop lost visitor income.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: What most influences where people go now?

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Viral TikToks and Instagram posts; social content often trumps guides. Influencers are used but organic posts sometimes have bigger reach.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Traditional travel journalism still matters for critical evaluation, but social media is hugely influential. Our paper still gets strong UK destination interest.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: Have you seen AI in travel?

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Yes — AI agents can copy itineraries from a video and personalise them using users' online data. Agents see it as a tool, not a total replacement for humans.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: Jamie, you mentioned weather apps affecting attendance. Explain that.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: Visitors check a single weather icon and may cancel if it shows rain. Research suggests that misinterpreted icons can cost attractions like Chester Zoo large sums in a single day.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: We want icons that show four points in the day (morning, lunchtime, afternoon, evening) so people make better decisions about visiting.

chapters.title: Workforce pressures, regulation and what Government could change
chapters.takeaway: Rising costs, low pay progression, transport gaps, regulation gaps for mixed organisations like zoos, and under-resourced national promotion need concrete Government action.

turns.speaker: Mr Bayo Alaba
turns.text: What stops recruiting and keeping staff?

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: Pay and progression: chefs are hard to recruit, and many leave for steadier roles. Zoos offer specialist careers but training is zoo-funded with little Government support.

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Staff housing, poor rural public transport and small allowances for staff accommodation make it hard. Many small businesses can't afford to house staff locally.

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Rising costs hit small hotels hard: Polizzi group saw nearly £1m added to costs from business rates, utilities, national insurance and wage rises — owners often don't pay themselves.

turns.speaker: Dr Rupa Huq
turns.text: What about short-term lets and tax fairness?

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Airbnbs undercut some businesses and benefit from different tax/relief rules; small B&Bs face heavy health and safety and letting rules but less favourable council tax treatment for second homes.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: Zoos fall between Departments: conservation and animal welfare sit with DEFRA, but we are also major employers, educators and regional economic drivers — we miss funding that heritage bodies access.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: Would a dedicated tourism Minister help?

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Yes — someone who understands and represents hospitality's issues. Also, create a professional centre of excellence to make hospitality an aspirational career.

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: For zoos, simplify Government contact by putting relevant responsibilities together so we don't fall through departmental cracks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If each of you could ask the Government for one change to help UK tourism in five years, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Jamie Christon
turns.text: Give sectors like zoos a clear, single departmental home so policy and funding fit what we actually do — conservation, education, tourism and scientific research in one place.

turns.speaker: Alex Polizzi
turns.text: Professionalise hospitality: invest in recognised training and a centre of excellence so the industry attracts and keeps skilled people and parents support careers in hospitality.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final points from the first panel?

turns.speaker: Vicky Philpott
turns.text: Affordability in school holidays and sewage pollution are the two big barriers for domestic coastal tourism.

turns.speaker: Chris Haslam
turns.text: Bathing-water quality is a reputational crisis: we risk being seen again as the 'sick man of Europe' if sewage issues aren't fixed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all — your evidence highlights concrete actions: fix coastal water quality, improve weather information, back season-extension, resolve regulatory gaps and invest in workforce training.
